name: Eleodes hispilabris
intro: I kept this western North American darkling beetle through two captive generations in a single colony bin. I left the eggs and young with the adults. A deep bed of desert sand with a little wood mixed through it gave me a practical way to raise successive generations without searching for individual eggs.

facts.title: Range
facts.text: Western North America, from western Canada south to Arizona and Texas

sections.title: Colony
sections.text:
I used a 20-quart bin and filled it about halfway with Exo Terra desert sand. I mixed a small amount of wood into the sand, then set pieces of bark on top. The wood was a minor part of the mixture. The adults lived and laid in this same enclosure.
I left the eggs where the females laid them. The eggs hatched in the adult enclosure. Substrate moisture was the detail I watched. I kept the sand from drying out completely, while also avoiding soaking it. I did not need separate incubation cups to get the next generation.

sections.title: Diet
sections.text: I fed the beetles fish flakes and dog food. By August 2025 this arrangement had carried the culture through two generations. I followed the colony as a group, so I cannot attach a clutch size or a precise time from egg to adult to any one female.

distribution.caption: Published records span the Canadian prairies, the western and central United States, and northern Mexico.
distribution.alt: Documented regions for Eleodes hispilabris: Alberta, Arizona, California, Chihuahua, Coahuila, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Manitoba, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Nuevo León, Oklahoma, Oregon, Saskatchewan, Sonora, South Dakota, Tamaulipas, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wyoming.
